title: Chapter 53 — The Gam
paragraphs: The ostensible reason why Ahab did not go on board the whaler we had spoken — that is, hailed at sea — was this: the wind and sea signaled storms. But even had this not been the case, he would not, perhaps, have boarded her after all — judging by his later conduct on similar occasions — if it had turned out that by hailing he had got a negative answer to the question he put. For, as it eventually turned out, he did not care to keep company, even for five minutes, with any stranger captain unless that captain could contribute some of the information he so absorbingly sought. But all this might not be properly appreciated unless something were said here about the peculiar customs of whaling vessels when they meet each other in foreign seas, and especially on a common cruising-ground.

If two strangers crossing the Pine Barrens in New York State, or the equally desolate Salisbury Plain in England — if, meeting each other by chance in such inhospitable wilds, these two cannot for the life of them avoid a mutual greeting, stopping for a moment to exchange the news, and perhaps sitting down for a while to rest together — then how much more natural that on the boundless Pine Barrens and Salisbury Plains of the sea, two whaling vessels sighting each other at the ends of the earth — off lonely Fanning's Island, or the faraway King's Mills — how much more natural, I say, that in such circumstances these ships should not only exchange hails, but come into still closer, more friendly and sociable contact. And this would seem especially a matter of course in the case of vessels owned in the same seaport, whose captains, officers, and not a few of the men know each other personally, and consequently have all sorts of dear domestic things to talk about.

For the long-absent ship, the outward-bound one perhaps has letters on board; at any rate, she will be sure to let her have some newspapers dated a year or two later than the last one in her blurred and thumb-worn files. And in return for that courtesy, the outward-bound ship would receive the latest whaling news from the cruising-ground she may be headed for, a thing of the utmost importance to her. And to some degree all this holds true of whaling vessels crossing each other's track on the cruising-ground itself, even though they are equally long absent from home. For one of them may have received a transfer of letters from some third vessel, now far away, and some of those letters may be for the people of the ship she now meets. Besides, they would exchange the whaling news and have a pleasant chat. For not only would they meet with all the sympathies of sailors, but also with all the special fellow-feeling that comes from a common pursuit and from hardships and dangers shared together.

Nor would difference of country make any very essential difference — that is, so long as both parties speak one language, as is the case with Americans and English. Though, to be sure, since there are so few English whalers, such meetings do not happen very often, and when they do, there is all too likely to be a sort of shyness between them; for your Englishman is rather reserved, and your Yankee doesn't care for that sort of thing in anybody but himself. Besides, the English whalers sometimes put on a kind of metropolitan superiority over the American whalers, regarding the long, lean Nantucketer, with his nondescript provincialisms, as a sort of sea-peasant. But just where this superiority of the English whalemen really lies would be hard to say, seeing that the Yankees, collectively, kill more whales in one day than all the English, collectively, in ten years. But this is a harmless little foible in the English whale-hunters, which the Nantucketer does not take much to heart — probably because he knows that he has a few foibles himself.

So, then, we see that of all ships sailing the sea separately, the whalers have the most reason to be sociable — and they are. Some merchant ships, on the other hand, crossing each other's wake in the mid-Atlantic, will often pass on without so much as a single word of recognition, cutting each other dead on the high seas like a pair of dandies on Broadway, and all the while indulging, perhaps, in fussy criticism of each other's rig. As for men-of-war, when they happen to meet at sea, they first go through such a string of silly bowings and scrapings, such a dipping of flags, that there does not seem to be much downright hearty goodwill and brotherly love about it at all. As for slave-ships meeting — why, they are in such a tremendous hurry that they run away from each other as soon as possible. And as for pirates, when they happen to cross each other's cross-bones, the first hail is "How many skulls?" — the same way whalers hail "How many barrels?" And once that question is answered, pirates steer apart at once, for they are infernal villains on both sides and don't like to see too much of each other's villainous likenesses.

But look at the godly, honest, unpretentious, hospitable, sociable, free-and-easy whaler! What does the whaler do when she meets another whaler in any sort of decent weather? She has a "Gam," a thing so utterly unknown to all other ships that they have never even heard the name; and if by chance they should hear of it, they only grin at it and repeat gamesome stuff about "spouters" and "blubber-boilers," and such pretty exclamations. Why all merchant seamen, and also all pirates and man-of-war's men and slave-ship sailors, should cherish such a scornful feeling toward whale-ships is a question it would be hard to answer. Because, in the case of pirates, say, I should like to know whether that profession of theirs has any special glory about it. It sometimes ends in uncommon elevation, it's true — but only at the gallows. And besides, when a man is elevated in that odd fashion, he has no proper foundation for his superior altitude. Hence I conclude that in boasting of being lifted high above a whaleman, the pirate has no solid basis to stand on.

But what is a Gam? You might wear out your index finger running up and down the columns of dictionaries and never find the word. Dr. Johnson never attained that much learning; Noah Webster's ark does not hold it. Nevertheless, this same expressive word has now been in constant use for many years among some fifteen thousand true-born Yankees. Certainly it needs a definition, and should be entered in the Lexicon. With that in view, let me learnedly define it.

GAM. Noun — A social meeting of two (or more) whale-ships, generally on a cruising-ground; when, after exchanging hails, they exchange visits by boats' crews: the two captains remaining, for the time, on board of one ship, and the two chief mates on the other.

There is one more small point about gamming that must not be forgotten here. Every profession has its own little peculiarities of detail, and so does the whale fishery. On a pirate ship, a man-of-war, or a slave ship, when the captain is rowed anywhere in his boat, he always sits in the stern sheets on a comfortable seat, sometimes a cushioned one, and often does his own steering with a pretty little milliner's tiller trimmed with bright cords and ribbons. But the whale-boat has no seat in the stern, no sofa of any kind, and no tiller at all. It would be a fine state of affairs indeed if whaling captains were wheeled over the water on casters, like gouty old aldermen in patent chairs. As for a tiller, the whale-boat never stands for any such effeminacy. So, since a whole boat's crew must leave the ship when gamming, and since the boat-steerer, or harpooner, is one of them, that subordinate does the steering on these occasions, and the captain, with nowhere to sit, is rowed off to his visit standing straight up like a pine tree. You will often notice that this standing captain, aware that the eyes of the whole visible world are fixed on him from the sides of both ships, is keenly conscious of how important it is to keep his dignity by keeping his feet. That is no easy matter. Behind him the huge projecting steering oar knocks him now and then in the small of the back, and in front the after-oar returns the compliment by rapping his knees. So he is wedged in completely, front and back, and can only widen himself sideways by settling down on his spread legs; but a sudden, violent pitch of the boat will often come close to toppling him, because a long foundation is worthless without a matching breadth. Just set two poles in a spread angle, and you will not be able to stand them up. Then again, it would never do — never, I say — for this straddling captain to be seen, in plain view of the world's riveted eyes, steadying himself the least bit by grabbing anything with his hands. In fact, to show his complete, buoyant self-command, he usually keeps his hands in his trouser pockets; though perhaps, since they are usually very large, heavy hands, he keeps them there as ballast. Still, there have been cases, and well-documented ones too, where a captain has been known, for an unusually critical moment or two — in a sudden squall, say — to grab the nearest oarsman's hair and hang on like grim death.
